newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand blasts Credit Lyonnais report on economy.
newsitem.headline: Thailand blasts Credit Lyonnais report on economy.

text.p: Thailand's central bank on Wednesday labelled as absurd and irresponsible a report issued this week by Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia saying that the country's economy would contract by one percent this year.

"Any forecast of a negative growth rate for Thailand this year is simply absurd and irresponsible, especially when the conclusion has been drawn from pure speculation and prejudice, without any due regard for macroeconomic analysis," the Bank of Thailand said in statement.
Credit Lyonnais' report published in the local media said it saw Thailand's 1997 economic growth shrinking by one percent, down from its earlier bearish forecast of 3.3 percent growth.
The firm said it had made the change because Thailand was in a depression and due to its costly struggle to defend its currency and the probability that interest rates would rise.
Thailand relied heavily on foreign capital and by recently imposing capital controls against baht speculation, the country had effectively shut out foreign inflows, Credit Lyonnais said.

Thailand has officially forecast 1997 growth at 5.9 percent, down from 6.4 percent in 1996 and the lowest in more than a decade. Private economists, however, have projected growth at anywhere between three to five percent.

The country's economy has braked sharply since last year, weighed down by sluggish exports, high interest rates that choke business activity and troubles in the cash-strapped finance and property sectors, analysts said.
The central bank said an economic slowdown in Thailand was a natural outcome after a very long period of high growth over the past decade.
"Emerging signs of overheating prompted the authorities to tighten monetary policy and trade off growth for stability, which has recently shown significant improvement," it added.
Inflation stood at 4.3 percent, affirming stability on the internal front, while first quarter 1997 current account deficits narrowed markedly by 38 percent from the corresponding period in 1996.
The central bank added that production in all sectors continued to expand and exports had improved since the beginning of this year and were set to expand further.
"With fundamental growth being observed, a negative economic growth for 1997 is an unlikely outcome," it said.

The bank said measures to deter speculation in the baht were specific and aimed at deterring speculative activities while allowing bona fide international trade and investment activities to proceed as normal.
"It is not true, however, that foreign capital has been the only source of financing of the Thai economy," it said.
The authorities had implemented short- and long-term measures to maintain liquidity and solvency and restructuring of the economy, it said.
"These policy measures will take some time to materialise. After this period of adjustment the Thai economy should resume its sustainable growth path," it added.
